subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: One mole of a substance contains:
choices: 22.7 dm³ of the substance at any temperature
12 g of the substance, whatever it is
items.note: The Avogadro constant gives the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions, formula units) per mole. Molar mass and molar volume depend on the substance or conditions.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: What is the molar mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ar: Ca 40.08, C 12.01, O 16.00)
items.note: 40.08 + 12.01 + 3 × 16.00 = 100.09. Common slips: counting one O (68.09) or two O (84.09).

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: How many moles are in 25.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.09 g mol⁻¹)?
items.note: n = m ÷ M = 25.0 ÷ 100.09 = 0.250 mol. Inverting (M ÷ m) gives 4.00.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: How many atoms are in 9.01 g of water (M = 18.02 g mol⁻¹)?
items.note: 9.01 g = 0.500 mol H₂O = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules; each molecule has 3 atoms, so 9.03 × 10²³ atoms. Read whether the question asks for molecules or atoms.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.note: Divide by Ar: C 3.33, H 6.63, O 3.33. Divide by the smallest: 1 : 2 : 1 → CH₂O.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 180.18 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is:
items.note: Mass of CH₂O unit = 30.03; 180.18 ÷ 30.03 = 6, so multiply every subscript by 6.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: 2.00 g of NaOH (M = 40.00 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved to make 250.0 cm³ of solution. What is its concentration?
items.note: n = 0.0500 mol; V = 0.2500 dm³; c = 0.0500 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³. Convert cm³ to dm³ (÷ 1000) before dividing.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: Equal volumes of two different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain:
items.note: Avogadro's law: equal volumes, same T and p → same amount (mol) of gas particles. Masses differ because molar masses differ; atom counts differ if molecules have different atomicity.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol dm⁻³ HCl is diluted with water to 100.0 cm³. What is the new concentration?
items.note: Amount stays the same: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, so 0.400 × 25.0 = c₂ × 100.0 → c₂ = 0.100. The 0.133 trap uses 75 cm³ (water added) instead of the final volume.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: Which sample contains the greatest number of oxygen atoms?
items.note: O atoms: Mg(NO₃)₂ 0.20 × 6 = 1.2 mol; CO₂ 0.60; H₂O 0.50; H₂SO₄ 0.40. Multiply by the count per formula unit.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: A hydrated salt CuSO₄·xH₂O loses 36.1% of its mass when heated to constant mass. What is x? (M CuSO₄ = 159.62, H₂O = 18.02)

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: 0.500 g of an oxide of iron contains 0.350 g of iron. Determine the empirical formula of the oxide. (Ar: Fe 55.85, O 16.00). Show your working.
items.tactic: Empirical formula: mass → moles → divide by smallest → convert to whole numbers (×2 when you get .5).

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: Outline how you would prepare 250.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ standard solution of sodium carbonate (M = 105.99 g mol⁻¹).
markscheme: Dissolve in a small volume of distilled water in a beaker, then transfer to a 250.0 cm³ volumetric flask with rinsings (1)
Make up to the mark with distilled water (meniscus on the line) and invert to mix (1)
items.tactic: Practical outlines: quantity, equipment by name, and the step that makes it accurate.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem: Explain why the molar volume of an ideal gas is the same for all gases at a given temperature and pressure, but the molar mass is not.
markscheme: Gas particles are far apart, so the volume is mainly empty space (1)
The size of the particles is negligible, so volume depends only on number of particles (T and p fixed) (1)
Molar mass depends on the mass of each particle, which differs between substances (1)
items.tactic: Link each property to what it depends on: particle count vs particle mass.

items.topicLabel: S1.4 Counting particles by mass: the mole
items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student heats an invented hydrated salt, MX·nH₂O (M of MX = 120.0 g mol⁻¹), to constant mass. Mass of crucible 21.450 g; crucible + hydrated salt 24.602 g; after 1st heating 23.400 g; after 2nd 23.250 g; after 3rd 23.250 g.
(a) Explain why the student heated three times. (b) Calculate n. (c) Suggest how the value of n would change if some salt spat out of the crucible during heating, and why.
markscheme: (a) To check that all the water has been removed: mass stops changing (constant mass) (1)
(c) Mass lost would be too large, so calculated water too large and n too high (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
